subject: Mathematics: Applications & Interpretation

questions.label: Hard
body: A platform's users are modelled by U(t)=1200/(1+Ae<sup>-kt</sup>). A proposed model has K=1200, A=8, k=0.22, with t in months.
questions.title: Fitting a logistic model

parts.label: a
parts.html: Calculate U(0), U(4), U(8) and U(12).

parts.label: b
parts.html: Show that ln(K/U-1)=ln A-kt and explain how this can be used to test the model.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the month when the model first reaches 90% of carrying capacity.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find the maximum monthly growth rate and when it occurs.

parts.label: e
parts.html: A measured value at t=8 is 4% below the model. Find the residual measured-model.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Discuss one strength and two limitations of using this model for long-term forecasting.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: The model gives U(0)=133, U(4)=278, U(8)=505, U(12)=764.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Rearranging gives K/U-1=Ae<sup>-kt</sup>; taking logs gives the result. A plot of ln(K/U-1) against t should be approximately linear, with intercept ln A and gradient -k.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Set U=0.9K. Then Ae-kt=1/9, so t=ln(9A)/k≈19.4 months.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Logistic growth is fastest at U=K/2=600.0. The time is ln A/k≈9.45, and the maximum rate is kK/4≈66 users per month.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Measured=0.96U(8)≈485. Residual=measured-model=-0.04U(8)≈-20.2.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html:
Strength: it represents early growth and eventual saturation with interpretable parameters.
Limitations include assuming a constant carrying capacity and growth parameter, ignoring shocks or seasonality, and extrapolating beyond the observed data range.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.label: d

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find the radius of the circle centred at V through the three sites.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Explain when V is a suitable candidate for a new facility intended to be far from all existing sites, and state one boundary check required in a finite region.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: The distances to A, B and C are approximately 5.07, 5.07 and 4.9. Hence C is closest.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: AB is horizontal and its midpoint is (4.5,0), so the bisector is x=4.5.

solparts.label: c

body: A network has weighted edges AB=4, AC=7, BC=2, BD=6, CD=3, CE=8, DE=4, BE=10.

parts.label: a
parts.html: State the degree of each vertex.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the shortest path from A to E.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Determine whether the original network has an Eulerian trail or circuit.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Explain how a route-inspection solution would be found if every edge must be traversed and the route must return to A.

parts.label: f
parts.html: A new edge AE of weight 5 is proposed. Explain how it could affect the shortest path and the minimum spanning tree, and perform both checks.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: The degrees are A:2, B:4, C:4, D:3, E:3.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Choose edges in increasing order while avoiding cycles. One MST is BC, CD, AB, DE, with total weight 13.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Dijkstra's algorithm gives A-B-C-D-E with total weight 13.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: The odd-degree vertices are D, E. A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit with zero odd vertices and a trail with exactly two; apply this rule to classify the network.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Pair the odd-degree vertices using shortest-path distances so that the added total is minimal. Duplicate those paths, making all degrees even, then find an Eulerian circuit beginning at A.

solparts.label: f

body: The column transition matrix is T=[[0.78,0.24],[0.22,0.76]]. Initially the state vector is v0=[0.65,0.35]ᵀ.
questions.title: A two-state Markov model

parts.label: a
parts.html: Verify that T is a stochastic matrix and interpret its first column.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Calculate v1 and v2.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the steady-state vector.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find v<sub>8</sub>.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Explain the role of the second eigenvalue and determine the long-run behaviour.

parts.label: f
parts.html: State two assumptions of this model and describe how each could fail in practice.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Each entry is non-negative and each column sums to 1. The first column means an item currently in state A remains in A with probability 0.78 and moves to B with probability 0.22.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Matrix multiplication gives A proportions a1=0.591 and a2=0.559; each B proportion is one minus the A proportion.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Solve Ts=s with entries summing to 1. The A proportion is q/(1-p+q)=0.522, so s=[0.522,0.478]ᵀ.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: For a two-state chain, an=a*+(a0-a*)(0.54)n. Hence v8≈[0.523,0.477]ᵀ.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: The eigenvalues are 1 and p-q=0.54. Since |p-q|<1, the transient term decays geometrically, so every initial distribution converges to the steady state.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: The transition probabilities are assumed constant over time and depend only on the current state. They can fail if policy, seasonality or learning changes the probabilities, or if earlier history affects future transitions.

questions.label: Hard
body: A survey gives the 2x2 observed table [[36, 24], [20, 40]]. The rows represent two teaching methods and the columns represent pass/fail.
questions.title: Testing association

parts.label: a
parts.html: State suitable null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Calculate the expected frequencies.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Calculate the chi-squared statistic and degrees of freedom.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Find the p-value and state the 5% conclusion.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Calculate phi as an effect-size measure and interpret its role.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Describe a Type I error in context and explain why statistical association does not prove causation.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: H0: teaching method and outcome are independent. H1: teaching method and outcome are associated.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Using E=(row total)(column total)/grand total gives [[28,32],[28,32]].

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: χ²=Σ(O-E)²/E≈8.57. Degrees of freedom=(2-1)(2-1)=1.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: For df=1, p≈0.00341. Therefore reject H0; there is evidence of association.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: φ=√(χ²/N)=0.267. It describes strength rather than only statistical significance; context and sample size should also inform interpretation.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: A Type I error is concluding that method and outcome are associated when they are actually independent. Association alone does not rule out confounding, selection effects or other causal explanations.

body: An object cools according to dT/dt=-0.12(T-18), with T(0)=88°C.
questions.title: Cooling with Euler's method

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain the sign of dT/dt while T is above ambient temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Use Euler's method with step h=2 to find approximations from t=0 to t=10.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Solve the differential equation exactly.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Compare the Euler and exact values at t=10 and calculate the error.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Find when the exact model first reaches 40°C.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Explain the effect of halving the Euler step size and discuss one limitation of Newton's law of cooling.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: When T>18, T-18>0, so dT/dt<0. The temperature decreases toward ambient.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: The recurrence is Tn+1=Tn-2k(Tn-A). Values are T(0)≈88, T(2)≈71.2, T(4)≈58.4, T(6)≈48.7, T(8)≈41.4, T(10)≈35.7.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Separating variables gives ln|T-18|=-0.12t+C. Using T(0)=88, T=18+70e-0.12t.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Euler gives 35.7; exact T(10)=39.1. Euler-exact≈-3.33°C.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Solve 40-18=(70)e-kt, giving t≈9.65.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: A smaller step normally reduces global numerical error because the slope is updated more often, at the cost of more calculations. The model assumes constant ambient temperature and a heat-transfer coefficient that does not vary with temperature, airflow or phase changes.

body: Points are represented by complex numbers and transformed by z<sub>n+1</sub>=wz<sub>n</sub>+c, where |w|=0.75, arg(w)=π/6, c=4+2i and z0=1-2i.
questions.title: An iterated rotation and dilation

parts.label: a
parts.html: Describe geometrically the multiplication by w.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Calculate z1 and z2 in Cartesian form.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Find the fixed point z* of the transformation.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Show that z_n-z*=w^n(z0-z*).

parts.label: e
parts.html: Determine the long-run behaviour and the distance from z_n to z*.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Write the real 2x2 matrix corresponding to multiplication by w and state its determinant.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: It is a rotation through π/6 anticlockwise about the origin combined with a dilation of scale factor 0.75.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Direct complex calculation gives z1≈5.4+1.08i and z2≈7.1+4.72i.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: At a fixed point, z*=wz*+c, so z*=c/(1-w)≈2.47+8.35i.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Subtract the fixed-point equation from the recurrence: z<sub>n+1</sub>-z*=w(z<sub>n</sub>-z*). Iterating gives the stated result.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Because |w|=0.75<1, wⁿ→0, so z_n→z*. Moreover |z_n-z*|=10.5(0.75)n.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: The matrix is [[0.65,-0.375],[0.375,0.65]]. Its determinant is |w|²=0.562, the area scale factor.

body: In each trial, success has probability p=0.28. Let X be the number of successes in n=12 independent trials.
questions.title: A binomial simulation

parts.label: a
parts.html: State the distribution, mean and variance of X.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Find P(X≥5) exactly using technology.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Describe a simulation algorithm using random numbers from 0 to 1.

parts.label: d
parts.html: For 5000 repetitions, estimate the standard error of the simulated event proportion.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Construct an approximate 95% interval for a simulation result equal to the exact probability.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Explain how increasing repetitions and using a fixed random seed affect the study.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: X~B(12,0.28), E(X)=np=3.36, Var(X)=np(1-p)=2.42.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Use 1-binomialCDF(12,0.28,4). The probability is 0.225.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Generate 12 independent U(0,1) values; count a success whenever U<0.28; record whether the count is at least 5; repeat many times and use the event proportion.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Using the exact probability as an estimate, SE=√[p(1-p)/5000]≈0.00591.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Approximate interval is p±1.96SE=[0.214,0.237].

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: Increasing repetitions reduces standard error in proportion to 1/√N but costs more computation. A fixed seed makes results reproducible for checking, but it does not make the sample more random or remove Monte Carlo error.

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Each entry is non-negative and each column sums to 1. The first column means an item currently in state A remains in A with probability 0.74 and moves to B with probability 0.26.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Matrix multiplication gives A proportions a1=0.543 and a2=0.521; each B proportion is one minus the A proportion.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Solve Ts=s with entries summing to 1. The A proportion is q/(1-p+q)=0.5, so s=[0.5,0.5]ᵀ.

solparts.label: d

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: The eigenvalues are 1 and p-q=0.48. Since |p-q|<1, the transient term decays geometrically, so every initial distribution converges to the steady state.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: The transition probabilities are assumed constant over time and depend only on the current state. They can fail if policy, seasonality or learning changes the probabilities, or if earlier history affects future transitions.
